questions.question: Explain the state's four instruments in the market with the consequence each one carries, arguing the minimum wage from both sides.
questions.expected_answer: A tax loads a cost onto each unit, shifting supply left and up: higher price, smaller quantity, burden shared — used deliberately against goods like cigarettes and sugary drinks. A subsidy or zero-rating carries part of the cost for producers or consumers, shifting supply right and down: lower price, larger quantity — the logic of VAT-free brown bread, maize meal and rice against the standard fifteen percent. A maximum price pinned below equilibrium keeps essentials affordable but opens a permanent shortage, since the price may not rise to close the gap: queues, rationing and black markets follow; a ceiling above equilibrium binds nothing. A minimum price pinned above equilibrium protects producers but leaves a standing surplus the state must buy, store or export. The minimum wage is the labour market's floor: it raises earnings for workers who keep employment, while a wage above market-clearing can reduce the number of workers hired — protection and pressure must both be stated.

questions.question: Tell the evolution of markets in five stages, naming the problem each stage solved, and give money's four functions.
questions.expected_answer: Self-sufficiency: households produce all they consume — no surplus, trade or specialisation, which keeps such societies poor. Surplus and barter: better tools create excess that seeks exchange, but barter drags the double coincidence of wants — each party must want exactly what the other offers at the same time, as with the herder whose goat nobody wants — keeping trade small and local. Money solves it: whatever is generally accepted works, serving as medium of exchange (dissolving the double coincidence), unit of account (one measure prices everything), store of value (surplus can wait), and standard of deferred payment (debts and credit become possible). Government enters as markets grow: trusted currency, enforced contracts, honest weights and measures, roads and courts, funded by taxing trade. Industrialisation: machines and factories multiply output and pull labour into towns — in South Africa through the mineral revolution, diamonds then gold dragging railways, capital and workers inland and entrenching migrant labour.

questions.question: Fence the labour force, match the three anchor statutes and the dispute ladder to their jobs, and compress unemployment and redress into their exam skeletons.
questions.expected_answer: Labour force: everyone aged fifteen to sixty-four who is employed or unemployed and actively seeking; learners, homemakers, retirees and the discouraged fall outside. Demand for labour is derived — firms hire because customers buy the product; supply comes from households; the wage forms where they meet. Statutes: Basic Conditions of Employment lays the floor under every contract — hours, leave, notice, no child labour; Labour Relations governs unions, collective bargaining, protected strikes and lock-outs; Employment Equity prohibits unfair discrimination and requires correction of past exclusion. Disputes climb bargaining, conciliation at the CCMA, binding arbitration, then the Labour Court for law. Unemployment: strict versus expanded definitions, rate divided by labour force; five types — frictional, structural (dominant), cyclical, seasonal, technological — each with its own remedy; consequences across person, economy and society; responses of production growth, public employment programmes and unemployment insurance. Redress: land restitution, redistribution and tenure; employment equity and skills; broad-based ownership, procurement and finance; small-business support — every instrument needing its partner support, with NEDLAC seating government, business, labour and community before major laws reach Parliament.
